content.heading: 6.3 Orthogonal Projections
content.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of a point in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ onto a line through the origin has an important analogue in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Given a vector $\textbf{y}$ and a subspace $W$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, there is a vector $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ in $W$ such that (1) $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is the unique vector in $W$ for which $\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is orthogonal to $W$, and (2) $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is the unique vector in $W$ closest to $\textbf{y}$. See Figure 1. These two properties of $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ provide the key to finding least-squares solutions of linear systems.

image.alt: A figure shows a horizontal plane W with two vectors projecting from point 0 on the plane in the form of a right-angled triangle.

where $\textbf{z}_{1}$ is a linear combination of some of the $\mathbf{u}_{i}$ and $\textbf{z}_{2}$ is a linear combination of the rest of the $\mathbf{u}_{i}$. This idea is particularly useful when $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{n} \right\}$ is an orthogonal basis. Recall from Section 6.1 that $W^{\bot}$ denotes the set of all vectors orthogonal to a subspace $W$.

content.heading: Proof﻿
content.paragraph: Let $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ be any orthogonal basis for $W$, and define $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ by (2).1 Then $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is in $W$ because $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is a linear combination of the basis $\mathbf{u}_{1}$, $\ldots$, $\mathbf{u}_{p}$. Let $\textbf{z} = \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$. Since $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}_{2}$, $\ldots$, $\mathbf{u}_{p}$, it follows from ($2$) that

Thus $\textbf{z}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}_{1}$. Similarly, $\textbf{z}$ is orthogonal to each $\mathbf{u}_{j}$ in the basis for $W$. Hence $\textbf{z}$ is orthogonal to every vector in $W$. That is, $\textbf{z}$ is in $W^{\bot}$.

To show that the decomposition in (1) is unique, suppose $\textbf{y}$ can also be written as $\textbf{y} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{1}$, with ${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$ in $W$ and $\textbf{z}_{1}$ in $W^{\bot}$. Then $\widehat{\textbf{y}} + \textbf{z} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{1}$ (since both sides equal $\textbf{y}$), and so

This equality shows that the vector $\mathbf{v} = \widehat{\textbf{y}} - {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$ is in $W$ and in $W^{\bot}$ (because $\textbf{z}_{1}$ and $\textbf{z}$ are both in $W^{\bot}$, and $W^{\bot}$ is a subspace). Hence $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$, which shows that $\mathbf{v} = \textbf{0}$. This proves that $\widehat{\textbf{y}} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$ and also $\textbf{z}_{1} = \textbf{z}$.
The uniqueness of the decomposition (1) shows that the orthogonal projection $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ depends only on $W$ and not on the particular basis used in (2).

content.heading: A Geometric Interpretation of the Orthogonal Projection
content.paragraph: When $W$ is a one-dimensional subspace, the formula (2) for $\text{proj}_{W}\mspace{2mu}\textbf{y}$ contains just one term. Thus, when $\dim W > 1$, each term in (2) is itself an orthogonal projection of $\textbf{y}$ onto a one-dimensional subspace spanned by one of the $\mathbf{u}’s$ in the basis for $W$. Figure 3 illustrates this when $W$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ spanned by $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{2}$. Here ${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$ and ${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{2}$ denote the projections of $\textbf{y}$ onto the lines spanned by $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{2}$, respectively. The orthogonal projection $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ of $\textbf{y}$ onto $W$ is the sum of the projections of $\textbf{y}$ onto one-dimensional subspaces that are orthogonal to each other. The vector $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ in Figure 3 corresponds to the vector $\textbf{y}$ in Figure 4 of Section 6.2, because now it is $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ that is in $W$.

figure.caption: The orthogonal projection of y ﻿is the sum of its projections onto one-dimensional subspaces that are mutually orthogonal

content.heading: Properties of Orthogonal Projections
content.paragraph: If $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $W$ and if $\textbf{y}$ happens to be in $W$, then the formula for $\text{proj}_{W}\mspace{2mu}\textbf{y}$ is exactly the same as the representation of $\textbf{y}$ given in Theorem 5 in Section 6.2. In this case, $\text{proj}_{W}\mspace{2mu}\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}$.
This fact also follows from the next theorem.

note.paragraph: Let $W$ be a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, let $\textbf{y}$ be any vector in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, and let $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ be the orthogonal projection of $\textbf{y}$ onto $W$. Then $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is the closest point in $W$ to $\textbf{y}$, in the sense that

content.paragraph: The vector $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ in Theorem 9 is called the best approximation to y by elements of W. Later sections in the text will examine problems where a given $\textbf{y}$ must be replaced, or approximated, by a vector $\mathbf{v}$ in some fixed subspace $W$. The distance from $\textbf{y}$ to $\mathbf{v}$, given by $\parallel \textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$, can be regarded as the “error” of using $\mathbf{v}$ in place of $\textbf{y}$. Theorem 9 says that this error is minimized when $\mathbf{v} = \widehat{\textbf{y}}$.

Inequality (3) leads to a new proof that $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ does not depend on the particular orthogonal basis used to compute it. If a different orthogonal basis for $W$ was used to construct an orthogonal projection of $\textbf{y}$, then this projection would also be the closest point in $W$ to $\textbf{y}$, namely $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$.

content.paragraph: Formula (4) follows immediately from (2) in Theorem 8. Also, (4) shows that $\text{proj}_{W}\text{\,\,}\textbf{y}$ is a linear combination of the columns of $U$ using the weights $\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}$, $\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{p}$. The weights can be written as $\mathbf{u}_{1}^{T}\textbf{y}$, $\mathbf{u}_{2}^{T}\textbf{y}$, $\ldots$, $\mathbf{u}_{p}^{T}\textbf{y}$, showing that they are the entries in $U^{T}\textbf{y}$ and justifying (5).
Suppose $U$ is an $n \times p$ matrix with orthonormal columns, and let $W$ be the column space of $U$. Then

If $U$ is an $n \times n$ (square) matrix with orthonormal columns, then $U$ is an orthogonal matrix, the column space $W$ is all of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, and $UU^{T}\textbf{y} = I\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}$ for all $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.

Although formula (4) is important for theoretical purposes, in practice it usually involves calculations with square roots of numbers (in the entries of the $\mathbf{u}_{i}$). Formula (2) is recommended for hand calculations.
